# Ice contributed only 53% to the flood triggered by the 2026 Langtang Lirung rock-ice avalanche in Nepal

- October 2026

## Abstract and Figures

A high-mountain rock-ice collapse can generate cascading debris flows and floods beyond its source. Quantifying the materials released at the source and those added to the flood along the corridor is essential to understanding the cascading event and disaster risk. We reconstruct the 26 August 2026 Langtang Lirung avalanche using satellite imagery, terrain reconstruction, videos, seismic scaling and river-gauge records. A source volume of 78.37 × 10⁶m³ and rock:ice volume ratio of 9:1 yield a mass of 1.98 × 10¹¹kg and a predicted magnitude of 5.20, consistent with the USGS observation. Complete ice melting supplies at most 7.19 × 10⁶m³, or 53% of the Devghat excess. Adding corridor-water storage gives (14.42 ± 0.80) × 10⁶m³, 6.30% above the observed 13.57 × 10⁶m³. The paired comparisons support debris-driven mobilization of pre-existing river water into a downstream surge. Hazard assessment and transboundary preparedness must incorporate corridor water and erodible deposits alongside unstable high-elevation sources.

Abstract 14 

A high-mountain rock-ice collapse can generate cascading debris flows and floods beyond its source. 15 

Quantifying the materials released at the source and those added to the flood along the corridor is 16 

essential to understanding the cascading event and disaster risk. We reconstruct the 26 August 2026 17 

Langtang Lirung avalanche using satellite imagery, terrain reconstruction, videos, seismic scaling and 18 

river- gauge records. A source volume of 78.37 × 10⁶m³ and rock:ice volume ratio of 9:1 yield a mass 19 

of 1.98 × 10¹¹kg and a predicted magnitude of 5.20, consistent with the USGS observation. Complete 20 

ice melting supplies at most 7.19 × 10⁶m³, or 53% of the Devghat excess. Adding corridor-water storage 21 

gives (14.42 ± 0.80) × 10⁶m³, 6.30% above the observed 13.57 × 10⁶m³. The paired comparisons 22 

support debris-driven mobilization of pre-existing river water into a downstream surge. Hazard 23 

assessment and transboundary preparedness must incorporate corridor water and erodible deposits 24 

alongside unstable high-elevation sources. 25 

 26 

Steep valley walls, large elevation differences and fractured bedrock allow high-mountain slope 27 

failures to release large masses into confined corridors. Glacier retreat and changes in frozen ground 28 

can alter slope support, water movement and rock strength, while geological structu re determines 29 

where failure can develop 1,2. Once released, rock and ice can entrain sediment and water, extending 30 

the affected area well beyond the initial collapse. Reconstructing these cascades therefore requires 31 

observations that connect the source, transport corridor and downstream response 3. The 2021 Chamoli 32 

disaster demonstrated this cascading hazard: an ice-rock avalanche transformed into a mobile debris 33 

flow that severely damaged two hydropower projects and left more than 200 people dead or missing 4. 34 

This cascading hazard is particularly relevant as glacier ice loss across High Mountain Asia continues 35 

amid ongoing cli mate warming 5,6,7,8, while sparse permafrost observations in the Hindu Kush 36 

Himalaya 2 limit our understanding of slope destabilization. With growing concerns over destructive 37 

3 

glacier-related slope failures 9 and the warming-related destabilization and adaptation limits highlighted 38 

by the 2026 Nepal cascade 10, understanding how these cascading hazard processes interact and 39 

propagate downstream is essential for explaining the disproportionate impacts of high-mountain 40 

disaster cascades. 41 

Understanding why these cascading impacts extend far beyond the initial collapse requires examining 42 

how the moving mass interacts with materials and water along its path. Snow entr ainment influenced 43 

the runout and air-blast generation at Langtang in 2015 11, while reconstructions in Tibet and 44 

Switzerland linked long runout to low effective friction and the presence of water or ice within the 45 

moving mass 12,13. Experimental and field evidence further identifies water availability, corridor 46 

materials and topographic confinement as important controls on mobility 14. Together, these studies 47 

suggest that the severity and extent of cascading hazards depend not only on the initial failed mass, but 48 

also on the progressive entrainment and transformation of materials during propagation. 49 

Beyond the physical amplification of cascading hazards, the exposure of people and infrastructure 50 

along their propagation corridors can further magnify the consequences. Hydropower facilities, roads, 51 

bridges and settlements are often situated within narrow mou ntain valleys, placing them directly in the 52 

paths of avalanches, debris flows and floods 15. The 2021 Chamoli disaster illustrates how a localized 53 

slope failure can cause extensive damage to downstream infrastructure and communities 4. Studies of 54 

glacial-lake outburst floods similarly highlight the importance of water storage, hydrological 55 

connectivity and downstream exposure in determining disaster impacts 16,17,18,19. The timing of flood 56 

release and the connectivity of downstream corridors further in fluence the distribution of these 57 

impacts 20,21,22,23, while assessments linking unstable slopes to avalanches entering stored water 58 

demonstrate how multiple processes can combine to threaten exposed areas 24. Thus, the consequences 59 

of a cascading disaster depend not only on how hazards evolve and propagate, but also on what lies 60 

along their paths. 61 

4 

The interaction between cascading hazard processes and downstream exposure highlights the need to 62 

reconstruct how an initial slope failure develops into a far-reaching disaster. Process-chain modelling 63 

demonstrates that avalanche location and propagation corridor affect flood intensity 25, while studies of 64 

Blatten and Dharali establish the value of pre-event source observations for early warning and risk 65 

reduction 26,27. Understanding these cascades therefore requires connecting the initial release, the 66 

entrainment and mobilization of materials and water along the transport corridor, and the resulting 67 

downstream response. An event-scale reconstruction must constrain both the released rock-ice mass 68 

and the water mobilized along its corridor using observations of the same event. A remaining 69 

observational challenge is to test both ends of the same cascade: whether a reconstructed rock-ice 70 

inventory is compatible with the seismic signal of release? Whether the water available along its path 71 

is compatible with a downstream hydrograph? 72 

On 26 August 2026, a s lope on the north-facing flank o f Langtang Lirung failed and initiated a cascade 73 

through Lhende Khola, Bhote Koshi and the Trishuli valley, which USGS preliminarily recorded as a 74 

seismic event. Subsequent assessments documented debris-flow and flood impacts extending 75 

approximately 100km downstream, with severe damage to riverside buildings and roads connecting 76 

China and Nepal 28,29,30. Nepal’s flood technical report records the lo ss of upstream hydrological 77 

stations, including the Furke (Malekhu) station and its bridge, and continued observation of the flood 78 

farther downstream 31. 79 

The far-reaching destruction caused by this event underscores a funda mental challenge in 80 

understanding high-mountain disaster cascades: how a localized rock-ice collapse can evolve into a 81 

destructive flood that threatens infrastructure and communities far beyond its source. Addressing this 82 

challenge requires moving beyond the characterization of individual hazards to quantitatively linking 83 

the initial failure, the transformation of moving materials and the mobilization of river water within a 84 

unified source-to-flood framework. Here, we reconstruct the 26 August 2026 Langtang Lirung cascade 85 

5 

by integrating source reconstruction, propagation evidence and a corridor-water budget (Fig. 1). Pre- 86 

and post-event imagery constrain the failure geometry (Fig. 2), while terrain reconstruction and UAV- 87 

derived composition estimates quantify the released rock-ice mass and assess its consistency with the 88 

USGS-recorded seismic magnitude (Fig. 3). Video observations reveal the sequence of flow 89 

transformations, and Knowledge-Driven Flood Intelligent Monitoring (KDFIM)-constrained water 90 

accounting evaluates the contribution of pre-existing river water against the observed Devghat flood 91 

hydrograph (Fig. 4). Sensitivity analysis across varying rock-to-ice ratios further examines the 92 

robustness of these con straints (Fig. 5). By jointly testing the source mass against seismic observations 93 

and the available water volume against downstream hydrological measurements, this study provides 94 

an observation-constrained assessment of how rock-ice avalanches can mobilize river water and 95 

amplify flood hazards far beyond the initial collapse. Thi s framework advances the quantitative 96 

understanding of high-mountain disaster cascades and provides a basis for assessing cascading flood 97 

risks to downstream infrastructure and communities. 98 

Imagery resolves the released rock-ice body 99 

The source footprint was delineated by comparing pre- and post-event satellite imagery, as shown in 100 

Fig. 2. Sentinel-2 imagery acquired on 24 August 2026 shows the intact source rock-ice body, whereas 101 

Landsat-9 imagery from 26 August 2026 reveals the disappearance of the source rock-ice body and the 102 

newly exposed coll apse scar (Fig. 2B, C). The reconstructed source boundary was further examined 103 

using a high-resolution image acquired on 10 October 2017 (Fig. 2D). This historical image reveals a 104 

distinctly fractured and weathered rock zone, with its structural boundaries closely matching the 105 

mapped failure footprint, as shown in the enlarged view (Fig. 2E). The agreement between the pre- 106 

existing fracture pattern and the post-event collapse geometry provides additional evidence for the 107 

identification of a rock-ice block. Repeated melting, refreezing and seasonal ice loss may have 108 

6 

contributed to progressive fracture opening and reduced slope support, consistent with mechanisms 109 

proposed for the destabilization of the Chamoli source 32. 110 

Regional structural studies have documented tectonically deformed High Himalayan Gneiss in the 111 

Langtang Valley 33, providing geological context for the fractured rock mass observed in the historical 112 

imagery. These observations suggest that pre-existing structural weaknesses, potentially modified by 113 

freeze-thaw processes and ice loss, may have contributed to slope destabilization. The source geometry 114 

was therefore constrained primarily by the observed collapse scar and surrounding terrain, while rock- 115 

ice composition and density were considered separately to estimate the released mass. 116 

Source reconstruction and seismic comparison 117 

Integration of the source geometry constrained by the mapped outline and three reference surfaces 118 

gives a source volume of 78.37 × 10 6 m 3 (Fig. 3B). Field UAV image interpretation gives a rock:ice 119 

volume ratio of 9:1. With densities of 917kg m− 3 for ice and 2700kg m− 3 for rock 34, the bulk density is 120 

2.52 × 10 3 kg m− 3 and the mass is 1.98 × 10 11 kg. The empirical scaling of Ekström and Stark 35 yields a 121 

maximum force of 3.66 × 10 11 N and a predicted magnitude of 5.20, matching the USGS-reported 122 

M5.20 landslide signal 29. 123 

The three-dimensional terrain reconstruction reveals a steep and confined propagation corridor 124 

connecting the rock-ice source to Gyirong Port through Lhende Khola and Bhote Koshi (Fig. 3A). The 125 

corresponding longitudinal profile shows a pronounced elevation drop from approximately 5,152 m at 126 

the source to 1,823 m near Gyirong Port over a distance of about 2 0 km (Fig. 3C). The particularly 127 

steep upper section provided a substantial gravitational driving force for the initial descent, while the 128 

narrow valley geometry channelled the moving material towards the downstream river corridor. The 129 

three-dimensional voxel reconstruction, constrained by the mapped source boundary (Fig. 2) and three 130 

reference surfaces, defines the geometry and substantial volume of the released rock-ice body (Fig. 131 

3B). This establishes the large mass involved in the initial failure. 132 

7 

The combination of substantial released mass, pronounced topogr aphic relief and confined valley 133 

geometry indicates considerable gravitational energy available for rapid downslope transport. This 134 

energetic motion is captured by successive video frames showing the rapid advance of a dense, dust- 135 

bearing avalanche front within seconds (Fig. 3C1-C3). The extensive dust cloud reflects intense 136 

material disturbance during descent, while a subsequent frame records continued secondary rock-ice 137 

fall after the initial passage (Fig. 3C4). Together, the reconstructed terrain, source rock-ice body and 138 

direct video observations establish the conditions for highly mobile, energetic mass transport through 139 

the confined valley. As the moving debris entered the river corri dor, its momentum and interaction 140 

with channel materials provided a physical pathway for the entrainment and downstream displacement 141 

of pre-existing river water. These observations therefore support the proposed transition from an initial 142 

rock-ice avalanche to a cascading debris-flow and flood process, providing the physical basis for the 143 

subsequent quantitative assessment of river-water mobilization and downstream flood volume. 144 

Transformation into a debris-flow flood cascade 145 

The reconstructed cascade reveals a progressive transformation of material composition and energy 146 

transfer from the initial rock-ice avalanche to the downstream flood (Fig. 4A). During rap id descent, 147 

the released rock-ice mass fragmented into large rock blocks and granular debris, which entrained loose 148 

sediments and channel deposits along the propagation corridor. The resulting dense debris flow 149 

remained dominated by solid materials, whose considerable momentum drove intense interactions wi th 150 

the underlying riverbed and pre-existing water. As illustrated in Fig. 4A1, the advancing debris mas s 151 

scoured channel deposits, displaced river water and transferred momentum to the surrounding water, 152 

accelerating its downstream redistribution. As coarse materials progressively deposited, the moving 153 

mixture evolved into a hyperconcentrated flow and ultimately a water-dominated flood surge that 154 

continued beyond the principal debris-deposition zone. This sequence illustrates the transfer of 155 

gravitational energy through fragmentation, sediment entrainment and water mobilization, 156 

8 

transforming a localized slope failure into a far-reaching flood cascade. The underlying mechanisms 157 

of granular motion, erosion and momentum transfer are cons istent with previous experimental and field 158 

investigations 36,37,38, as well as observations of rock-avalanche-generated sediment flows 39 and the 159 

Chamoli disaster 4. 160 

The spatial reconstruction further establishes the propagation pathway and the potential exten t of 161 

debris-driven water mobilization (Fig. 4B). KDFIM-derived mapping identifies the aff ected river 162 

corridor and its flow-depth distribution 40,41, while DEM-based cumulative-energy analysis constrains 163 

the downstream reachability of the moving material according to established routing and friction 164 

principles 36,42,43,44,45. The resulting critical-friction field delineates the energetically reachable corrid or, 165 

with finite v alues of μcrit > 0.10 defining the adopted spatial domain for s olid-material influence under 166 

the specified friction constraint 36,42,43,44,45. This physically constrained domain identifies the river 167 

reaches potentially exposed to direct debris interaction, providing the spatial basis for estimating the 168 

pre-existing water available for mobilization. The recorded flood passage through the Bhote Koshi and 169 

Trishuli valleys further establishes the temporal continuity of downstream propagation towards 170 

Devghat 31,46. 171 

Independent hydrological observations provide evidence for the above spatial reconstruction. Water 172 

levels in the Kali Gandaki at Kota Gaon and Marsyangdi at Bimalnagar remained relatively stable 173 

during the event, without a corresponding flood pulse (Fig. 4B) 46. In contrast, Devghat recorded a 174 

pronounced flood surge following the documented passage through the avalanche-affected Trishuli 175 

corridor 31. This spatial contrast, together with the observed propagation sequence, identifies the 176 

upstream rock-ice avalanche cascade as the driver of the Devghat flood anomaly. 177 

The reconstructed wat er inventory provides a quantitative test of the above mec hanism. Hydraulic 178 

information from the UT-1 Disaster Management Plan 47, combined with KDFIM-derived pre-event 179 

water coverage, constrains the volume of river water within the debris-reachable corridor. 180 

9 

Independently, the reconstructed source composition defines the maximum potential meltwater 181 

supply 34. Even under complete melting, source ice accounts for only approximately 53% of the 182 

observed excess floodwater, demonstrating that ice melting alone is insufficient to explain the 183 

downstream response. Combining the source-ice meltwater limit with the estimated corridor-water 184 

inventory yields an available water volume of (14.42 ± 0.80) × 10⁶ m³, closely matching the 185 

independently derived Devghat excess 31 of 13.57 × 10⁶ m³. The small difference between these 186 

estimates supports the volumetric feasibility of debris-driven river-water mobilization under the 187 

adopted melting and water-delivery assumptions. 188 

Together, the reconstructed material transformations, spatially constrained debris reachability, 189 

tributary observations and downstream water-volume agreement provide converging evidence for the 190 

proposed flood-amplification mechanism. The initial rock-ice collapse supplied the mass and 191 

gravitational energy for rapid debris transport, while interactions with the river corridor enabled the 192 

mobilization and downstream redistribution of pre-existing water. This coupling between solid- 193 

material transport and river-water mobilization provi des a physical explanation for how a localized 194 

high-mountain slope failure generated a destructive flood extending far beyond the initial collapse area. 195 

Discussion 196 

The observational comparisons provide quantitative evidence on the reconstructed Langtang Lirung 197 

rock-ice avalanche and its downstream flood response. By using a single source-volume and 198 

composition parameterization, the reconstructed mass and potential water inventory can be evaluated 199 

against independently acquired seismic and hydrological observations. The composition sensitivity 200 

analysis (Fig. 5) shows that the UAV-derived rock-to-ice ratio of 9:1 produces the smallest absolute 201 

discrepancies in both predicted seismic magnitude and available floodwater volume among the nine 202 

tested scenarios. Increasing the ice fraction progressively reduces the predicted magnitude while 203 

10 

substantially increasing the potent ial meltwater supply. Even when the rock-to-ice ratio shifts to 8:2, 204 

the predicted seismic magnitude changes only slightly, whereas the estimated available water volume 205 

exceeds the observed excess floodwater volume by more than 50%. This contrasting sensitivity 206 

demonstrates that the hydrological comparison provides particularly strong evidence on the assumed 207 

ice fraction, whereas the seismic comparis on primarily evaluates the plausibility of the reconstructed 208 

moving mass. The agreement of both comparisons under the same source configuration strengthens the 209 

consistency of the reconstruction. 210 

More importantly, the reconstructed cascade reveals how the initial gravitational energy and substantial 211 

rock-ice mass can drive downstream flood a mplification through interactions with materials and water 212 

along the river corridor. During rapid descent, fragmentation and sediment entrainment transformed 213 

the initial avalanche into a dense debris flow capable of scouring channel deposits and transferring 214 

momentum to pre-existing river water. The resulting displacement and acceleration of river water 215 

concentrated part of the available water into a downstream-propagating surge, allowing the flood to 216 

extend beyond the principal deposition zone of coarse debris. This mechanism explains why the 217 

downstream flood response cannot be attributed to source-ice melting alone. The reconstructed 218 

corridor-water inventory, when combined with the maximum source-ice meltwater supply, closely 219 

approaches the independently estimated Devghat excess, with a central difference of only 6.30%. This 220 

quantitative correspondence supports the feasibility of debris-driven river-water mobilization as a 221 

major component of the cascading flood mechanism. 222 

Comparisons with other Himalayan disasters place this mechanism within a broader context of 223 

cascading hazard amplification. During the 2021 Chamoli disaster, approximately 20% of the released 224 

material consisted of ice, and melting contributed to the transformation of the initial rock-ice avalanche 225 

into a highly mobile sediment-laden flow 4. In the 2023 Sikkim disaster, the release of approximately 226 

50 × 10⁶ m³ of lake water was accompanied by extensive downstream erosion involving approximately 227 

11 

270 × 10⁶ m³ of sediment 48. Although these events involved different initial water sources and flow- 228 

transformation pathways, they demonstrate how interactions with stored water and erodible valley 229 

materials can substantially extend the consequences of an initial disturbance. The Langtang Lirung 230 

cascade adds a distinct perspective by quantitatively examining the potential contribution of pre- 231 

existing ri ver water, alongside source-ice melting. Its principal contribution lies in connecting this 232 

corridor-water inventory to both the reconstructed source mass and the downstream flood hydrograph 233 

through independent observational constraints. 234 

The Langtang Lirung disaster demonstrates how a localized rock-ice avalanche can evolve into a far- 235 

reaching flood cascade through the coupled transport of solid debris and river water. By combining 236 

source reconstruction with independent seismic and hydrological observations, this study constrains 237 

both the initial release and the potential water available for downstream flood formation. The results 238 

show that source-ice melting alone is insufficient to account for the observed floodwater excess, while 239 

mobilization of pre-existing ri ver water provides a quantitatively plausible explanation for the 240 

additional volume. This source-to-flood framework advances the understanding of high-mountain 241 

disaster amplification and highlights the need to incorporate river-water storage, sediment availability 242 

and downstream exposure into assessments of cas cading hazards. Under global warming, the retreat of 243 

snow and g lacier ice progressively reduces slope support and weakens ice-bonded rock masses. 244 

Extreme rainfall and major earthquakes can disturb these increasingly unstable slopes, increasing the 245 

risk of large cascading disasters across the Himalaya-Hindu Kush region. Connected river corridors 246 

transmit these hazards across national borders, making joint source-and-corridor ha zard surveys, shared 247 

satellite, seismic and hydrological observations, and coordinated regional preparedness essential. 248 

12 

Methods 249 

We reconstructed the source mass and available floodwater from imagery, terrain and external 250 

hydraulic information, then compared these outputs with separately acquired USGS seismic and 251 

Devghat discharge records (Fig. 1). The calculations and obser vational benchmarks are described 252 

below. 253 

Three-stream design and separation of evidence 254 

Stream A calculates source mass, long-period magnitude and available water using a single, well- 255 

defined set of source-volume and rock-to-ice ratio parameters. Stream B provides the USGS catalogue 256 

magnitude; Stream C calculates excess volume solely from the Devghat hydrograph. These 257 

observational benchmarks (B and C) do not enter the forward inventory equations. 258 

Data sources and spatiotemporal characteristics 259 

(1) Satellite imagery. Copernicus/ESA Sentinel-2 MultiSpectral Instrument (MSI) imagery acquired 260 

on 12 and 24 August 2026 provides the regional basemap and pre-failure source observations, 261 

respectively. Landsat-9 Operational Land Imager-2 (OLI-2) imagery acquired on 26 August 2026 262 

records the post-collapse scar. Historical image ry accessed through Google Earth and dated 10 October 263 

2017 provides the earlier structural view. Sentinel-2 and Landsat product specifications and access are 264 

provided by the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (https://dataspace.copernicus.eu/) and USGS 265 

EarthExplorer (https://earthexplorer.usgs.gov/), respectively. Post-event S AR imagery provided by the 266 

Changsha Tianyi Research Institute and Gaofen (GF) satellite imagery obtained from the Land Satellite 267 

Remote Sensing Application Cente r, Ministry of Natural Resources, were additionally used with 268 

KDFIM to reconstruct the flood-affected extent and inundation depth. 269 

(2) Elevation data and derived products. Elevation data were obtained from the Copernicus Digital 270 

Elevation Model (COP-DEM GLO-30), which provides global elevation information 271 

(https://doi.org/10.5270/ESA-c5d3d65). The elevation data were resa mpled to a 10m analysis grid. 272 

13 

KDFIM was implemented on this common 10m grid to integrate the multi-source observations and 273 

derive flood extent and depth. All derived raster products in thi s study, including the source- 274 

reconstruction, reachability, water-mask, flood-extent and depth layers, were output at 10m grid 275 

spacing. This harmonized output spacing supports cell-wise integration a nd water-volume accounting. 276 

(3) Seismic and hydrological observations. The USGS earthquake catalogue provides the 26 August 277 

2026 landslide event us7000tbwb, including its location, origin time and reported magnitude. Devghat 278 

discharge observations for 26 August 2026 were transcribed from the flood technical report issued by 279 

the Flood Forecasting Division, Hydrology and Water Resources Research Center, Water and Energy 280 

Commission Secretariat, Government of Nepal. The Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources 281 

Research Assessment Report II supplies the same- day water-level records for Kali Gandaki at Kota 282 

Gaon and Marsyangdi at Bimalnagar. 283

A simple analytical model was developed for evaluating the attenuation of flood wave peak discharge. The physically‐based model represents the flood wave along its trajectory, based on the diffusive model. Relative peak discharge decreases along the downstream distance according to a power function. The distance is scaled by the attenuation factor related to river hydrodynamics (flow rating, hydraulic diffusivity, celerity, and floodplain storage) and input hydrograph (initial peak discharge, hydrograph volume, and its relative curvature). It also informs the attenuation length, which is a practical indicator of the river distance in which discharge decreases by a given factor. Sensitivity analyses indicate that initial peak discharge, volume, floodplain storage, and slope are the governing factors of attenuation. Model's validity and accuracy were demonstrated by reproducing data from (a) numerical solutions of the Saint‐Venant equations covering a wide range of conditions, (b) 29 observations from 11 historical dam‐breaks, (c) 15 observations of natural floods in seven rivers and (d) a detailed hydrodynamic model. The model errors were generally lower than 10% and not larger than the typical uncertainty of flood observations. The accuracy is higher than simplified empirical models and analogous to a detailed hydrodynamic model that is representative of current practice. The proposed flood attenuation model can be easily applied using a few common parameters and a simple equation in a basic spreadsheet. It is suitable for practical applications such as first assessments of natural and dam‐break floods, engineering design, and analyses of large river networks supported by remote sensing data.

Erosion can significantly increase the destructive power of a landslide by amplifying its volume, mobility and impact force. The threat posed by an erosive landslide is linked to its mobility. No mechanical condition has yet been presented for when, how and how much energy erosive landslides gain or lose. Here, we pioneer a mechanical model for the energy budget of erosive landslides that controls enhanced or reduced mobility. Inertia is related to an entrainment velocity, is a fundamentally new understanding. This ascertains the true inertia of erosive landslides, making a breakthrough in correctly determining the landslide mobility. Erosion velocity, which regulates the energy budget, determines the enhanced or reduced mobility. Newly developed energy generator offers the first-ever mechanical quantification of erosional energy and a precise description of mobility. This addresses the long-standing question of why many erosive landslides generate higher mobility, while others reduce mobility. We demonstrate that erosion and entrainment are different processes. Landslides gain energy and enhance mobility if the erosion velocity exceeds the entrainment velocity. Energy velocity delineates distinct excess energy regimes. Newly introduced mobility scaling and erosion number deliver the explicit measure of mobility. Presented dynamical equations correctly include erosion induced net momentum production.

Tsunamis generated by deformable granular landslides are physically modeled in a three-dimensional tsunami wave basin based on the generalized Froude similarity. The dynamic landslide impact characteristics were controlled by means of a novel pneumatic landslide generator. The wave amplitudes, periods, and wavelengths are related to the landslide parameters at impact with the landslide Froude number being a dominant parameter. Between 1 and 15% of the landslide kinetic energy at impact is converted into the wave train energy. The wave amplitudes decay in radial and angular directions from the landslide axis. The first wave crest mostly travels with speeds close to the theoretical approximation of the solitary wave speed. The measured tsunami wave profiles were either of the nonlinear oscillatory or nonlinear transition type depending primarily on the landslide Froude number and relative slide thickness at impact. The generated waves range from shallow to deep water depth regimes, with the majority being in the intermediate water depth regime. Wave characteristics are compared with other two- and three-dimensional landslide tsunami studies and the results are discussed.

On 3 October 2023, a multihazard cascade in the Sikkim Himalaya, India, was triggered by 14.7 million cubic meters of frozen lateral moraine collapsing into South Lhonak Lake. The impact generated an ~20-meter tsunami-like impact wave, which breached the moraine and drained ~50 million cubic meters of the lake’s water. The ensuing glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) eroded ~270 million cubic meters of sediment, which overwhelmed infrastructure, including hydropower installations along the Teesta River. The physical scale and human and economic impacts of this event prompt urgent reflection on the role of climate change and human activities in exacerbating such disasters. Insights into multihazard evolution are pivotal for informing policy development, enhancing early warning systems (EWS), and spurring paradigm shifts in GLOF risk management strategies in the Himalaya and other mountain environments.

Rock avalanches, debris flows, and related phenomena consist of grain-fluid mixtures that move,across three-dimensional terrain. In all these phenomena,the same basic forces govern motion, but differing mixture compositions, initial conditions, and boundary,conditions yield varied dynamics,and deposits. To predict motion,of diverse grain-fluid masses from initiation to deposition, we develop a depth-averaged, three- dimensional,mathematical,model,that accounts,explicitly for solid- and fluid-phase forces and interactions. Model input consists of initial conditions, path topography, basal and internal friction angles of solid grains, viscosity of pore fluid, mixture density, and a mixture diffusivity that controls pore pressure dissipation. Because these properties are constrained by independent measurements, the model requires little or no calibration and yields readily testable predictions. In the limit of vanishing Coulomb,friction due to persistent high fluid pressure the model equations describe motion of viscous floods, and in the limit of vanishing fluid stress they describe one-phase granular avalanches. Analysis of intermediate,phenomena,such as debris flows and pyroclastic flows requires use of the full mixture equations, which can simulate interaction of high-friction surge fronts with more-fluid debris that follows. Special numerical,methods,(described in the companion paper) are necessary to solve the full equations, but exact analytical solutions of simplified equations,provide critical insight. An analytical solution for translational motion,of a Coulomb,mixture accelerating from rest and descending,a uniform,slope demonstrates that steady flow can occur only asymptotically. A solution for the asymptotic,limit of steady flow in a rectangular channel,explains why shear may,be concentrated,in narrow marginal,bands that border a plug of translating debris. Solutions for static equilibrium,of source areas describe conditions of incipient slope instability, and other static solutions show,that nonuniform,distributions of pore fluid pressure produce,bluntly tapered,vertical profiles at the margins,of deposits. Simplified equations,and solutions may,apply in additional situations identified by a scaling analysis. Assessment,of dimensionless,scaling parameters,also reveals that miniature,laboratory experiments,poorly simulate the dynamics,of full-scale flows in which fluid effects are significant. Therefore large geophysical,flows can exhibit dynamics,not evident at laboratory scales.

Rock, snow and ice masses are often dislodged on steep slopes of mountainous regions. The masses, which typically are in the form of innumerable discrete blocks or granules, initially accelerate down the slope until the angle of inclination of the bed approaches the horizontal and bed friction eventually brings them to rest. The present paper describes an initial investigation which considers the idealized problem of a finite mass of material released from rest on a rough inclined plane. The granular mass is treated as a frictional Coulomb-like continuum with a Coulomb-like basal friction law. Depth-averaged equations of motion are derived; they bear a superficial resemblance to the nonlinear shallow-water wave equations. Two similarity solutions are found for the motion. They both are of surprisingly simple analytical form and show a rather unanticipated behaviour. One has the form of a pile of granular material in the shape of a parabolic cap and the other has the form of anM-wave with vertical faces at the leading and trailing edges. The linear stability of the similarity solutions is studied. A restricted stability analysis, in which the spread is left unperturbed shows them to be stable, suggesting that mathematically both are possible asymptotic wave forms. Two numerical finite-difference schemes, one of Lagrangian, the other of Eulerian type, are presented. While the Eulerian technique is able to reproduce theM-wave similarity solution, it appears to give spurious results for more general initial conditions and the Lagrangian technique is best suited for the present problem. The numerical predictions are compared with laboratory experiments of Huber (1980) involving the motion of gravel released from rest on a rough inclined plane. Although in these experiments the continuum approximation breaks down at large times when the gravel layer is only a few particle diameters thick, the general features of the development of the gravel mass are well predicted by the numerical solutions.

Near-real-time flood maps are vital for efficiently coordinating emergency responses during flooding events. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellite remote sensing, lauded for its capacity to capture data day and night in diverse weather conditions, emerges as a leading tool for acquiring flood mapping information. However, in cross-regional flood monitoring, challenges in accurately detecting ... [Show full abstract] floodwater pixels arise from interference factors affecting SAR backscatter, which are inherently present in various geo-environments (e.g., wind waves, vegetation, thick clouds, and high-relief terrain). These factors include shadow and layover effects, as well as radar response areas that resemble water surfaces and land cover. To address these challenges, our study proposes the Sample-Adjusted Threshold Calculation (SATC) approach, which not only quantifies the impact of these interference factors but also enhances algorithm generalization and interpretability, effectively overcoming the limitations of regional specificity in flood mapping. SATC applies three layers of constraints, including sample space distribution, sample proportion and algorithm threshold space, to comprehensively calculate a flood segmentation threshold satisfying varied conditions involved in cross-regional flood monitoring. The experimental results of applying SATC to various scenarios indicate that these SATC-optimized algorithms achieve a notable 10-30% improvement in accuracy while concurrently reducing false and omission rates to <20%. Furthermore, incorporating SATC into the Knowledge-Driven Flood Intelligent Monitoring (KDFIM) framework yields optimal results, achieving a flood mapping accuracy >95% and a Kappa value >0.95. The reached KDFIM(SATC) facilitates heightened robustness and enables the rapid diagnosis and quantification of flood mapping details, achieving flood detection in just 0.3795s/100km². Overall, KDFIM(SATC) proves to be robust as a pivotal tool in emergency response efforts during flooding events.

Climate change-induced rainfalls have elevated the likelihood of flood occurrences, disrupting severely the normal functioning of people. Especially in the geographically unique Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei (BTH) plain in north China, an unanticipated sudden and long-duration flood-inundation happened in the summer of 2023 (referred to as the ‘23.7’ BTH flood). To address the dynamic information and ... [Show full abstract] recreate the flood evolution, we constructed a flood retrieving and analysis procedure to elucidate the development process and its impacts. First, accurately extract the temporal inundation extent of floods. Subsequently, we implemented the selected knowledge-driven algorithm to retrieve the dynamic information of flood evolution, including inundation extent, water depth, and shortest inundation duration. Furthermore, hazard-bearing bodies like cultivated land, population, and buildings were analyzed to improve our understanding of the flood impact. We uncovered that the ‘23.7’ BTH flood had caused extensive inundation and notably affected the Daqing River System, where the flood breached the river bank and submerged both buildings (0.96 km²) and cultivated land (241.46 km²), and led to prolonged inundation in the Baiyangdian area, which persisted for up to 30 days. This disastrous event highlights the great requirements to boost upstream flood storage capacity and enhance preparedness and rapid response capabilities for abnormal floods.

**Andrea Alejandra Drozd**: Principal Researcher @ Universidad Nacional de Avellaneda | Research, Environmental Data Analytics.

---

🛰️ Langtang, Nepal. Seven weeks of data describing a landscape with no margin left. What App Floods can tell you
A monitoring system doesn't predict a landslide. It does something more honest: it shows when a basin enters a state where any trigger will do.
This is what the dashboard showed between 5 July and 26 August 2026, over an AOI in Langtang Lirung:
🌡️ Air temperature — 96th percentile. Not a warm summer: one of the warmest on record. In a glacial valley, that means unaccounted water, released from above.
💧 Soil moisture at p85, but infiltration only normal (p62). The soil hit its ceiling: it no longer absorbs. Every excess goes overland → runoff at p81, water balance in sustained surplus.
Mechanically: pore pressure rises, shear strength drops.
🗺️ And the map — net primary productivity anomaly — adds the piece no average can show. The pattern isn't uniform:
▪️ On the valley floors, negative anomalies. Vegetation stressed by excess, not drought: roots starved of oxygen in waterlogged soil.
▪️ At high elevations, productivity surging. Ground that in a normal year would still lie under snow, exposed early and with meltwater available. The signature of above-normal melt.
The AOI closes at NPP p92 and NDVI p96. In isolation, that would look like an excellent season. It isn't: the average hides two opposing processes. The greening of the summits statistically offsets the decline in the valleys.
A fourth figure confirms it: vegetation water content sits at p31. Very green, with no notable leaf water content. Young, colonizing, shallow-rooted cover — the kind that contributes least to slope stability, precisely where the ground has just been left bare.
More exposed surface, more meltwater circulating, cover that doesn't hold. The monsoon arrived on top of that.
No single indicator on this list would have justified an alert on its own. The value lies in the convergence: five independent signals pointing the same way for seven weeks.
That's reaction time measured in weeks, not hours: reviewing access routes, prioritizing slope inspection, strengthening warnings in valley-floor settlements.
Predicting the exact moment of a landslide remains impracticable. Identifying that a basin has spent weeks operating outside its historical range — with open data, no ground instrumentation, for any polygon on the planet — no longer is.
#RemoteSensing #DisasterRiskReduction #ClimateChange #Himalaya
Analysis with appFloods over a custom AOI. Percentiles are computed against the historical climatology of the same seasonal window. The indicators describe predisposing conditions and statistical anomalies; they do not constitute a forecast of specific geomorphological events.

Anatomy of a Himalayan Disaster: How Bedrock Failure and Cryospheric Decay Triggered the Nepal-Tibet Flash Floods – The Green Outlet

# Anatomy of a Himalayan Disaster: How Bedrock Failure and Cryospheric Decay Triggered the Nepal-Tibet Flash Floods

 By Iffa Jayyana 

 September 16, 2026 

 

## Executive Overview

On the morning of 26 August, a catastrophic flash flood swept through the high-altitude borderlands connecting Nepal and the Chinese autonomous region of Tibet. The sudden surge destroyed communities, tore through vital infrastructure, and claimed more than 1,300 lives, with thousands more reported missing downstream. 

Initial reports attributed the tragedy to a conventional glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) or a direct glacier collapse. However, comprehensive scientific investigations—utilizing high-resolution satellite imagery, seismic telemetry, and regional climate data—have revealed a far more complex phenomenon: a multi-hazard cascade. 

The disaster began high on the slopes of Mount Langtang-Lirung, where a massive section of underlying bedrock collapsed, taking an overlying glacier with it. This massive landslide plunged more than 2,000 vertical meters, pulverizing ice and rock into a high-velocity slurry that choked transboundary river systems and breached multiple temporary debris dams.

```
[Bedrock Failure at 5,200m] 
         │
         ▼ (2,000m Fall)
[Ice/Rock Pulverization & Debris Lake]
         │
         ▼ (Lake Breach)
[High-Velocity Slurry: 30 km/h Surge]
         │
         ▼ (River Network Choked)
[Widespread Transboundary Devastation]
```

While climate skeptics seized upon the bedrock failure to downplay the influence of anthropogenic warming, glaciologists and geomorphologists emphasize that cryospheric degradation—specifically rapid permafrost thaw, severe glacier retreat, and record-breaking alpine temperatures—substantially destabilized the mountain. 

Economic damages are estimated to exceed $2.5 billion, underscoring the acute vulnerability of the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region to climate-accelerated disasters.

## Detailed Chronology & Reconstruction of Events

```
CHRONOLOGY OF DISASTER
========================================================================
26 Aug, 08:37 AM  ── Bedrock & glacier collapse on Langtang-Lirung.
                   ── USGS detects M4.4 seismic shock (later revised 
                      to M5.2-equivalent debris avalanche).
26 Aug, Morning   ── Debris lake forms on valley floor; subsequently 
                      bursts, releasing high-velocity mud/water surge.
26 Aug, 01:00 PM  ── Flood wave reaches Mugling (130 km downstream); 
                      Trishuli River rises 9 m in 30 minutes at Galchhi.
28 Aug            ── Secondary barrier lake in Tibet bursts, sending 
                      a second destructive surge downstream.
04 Sep            ── Official loss estimates published ($2.5B+ total).
========================================================================
```

### The Initial Instability (26 August, 08:37 AM Local Time)

The trigger occurred high in the Nepalese Himalaya on the sheer faces of Mount Langtang-Lirung. At approximately 5,200 meters above sea level, a massive structural block of deep bedrock fractured and sheared away from the mountain core. 

Sitting directly atop this rock mass was an alpine glacier, which was swept downward in the failure. The combined volume of rock, ice, and subglacial sediment fell nearly 2,200 vertical meters, crashing onto the valley floor at an elevation of 3,000 meters.

The mechanical force of this impact generated localized ground motion so intense that the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) automatically recorded a magnitude 4.4 earthquake at 08:37 AM local time. Subsequent analysis of the seismic signature led the USGS to reclassify the signal not as a tectonic quake, but as an ice-rock avalanche and mass flow equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.

### Lake Formation and Primary Outburst Surge

Upon impacting the valley floor, the kinetic energy of the collapse pulverized the ice and rock matrix, flash-melting portions of the ice and mixing with loose valley sediments. This dense material slammed into the Lhende Khola river—a transboundary watercourse known as the Donglin Tsangpo in China, which feeds into the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems in Nepal.

The initial mass movement temporarily dammed the river channel, creating a temporary debris lake. Within hours, the impounded water overtopped and breached this unstable dam. 

According to findings by the HiRisk scientific consortium, the resulting floodwave surged downstream at speeds reaching 30 kilometers per hour (19 mph). 

- In Galchhi, a municipality in Nepal’s Dhading district, the Trishuli River surged upward by nine meters in just 30 minutes.
- By 1:00 PM local time, the flood crest reached the town of Mugling, more than 130 kilometers downstream from the collapse site, sweeping away bridges, roads, and border posts along its path.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       TRANSBOUNDARY RIVER SYSTEM                      |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  Langtang-Lirung Massif (Collapse Site: 5,200m)                       |
|    │                                                                  |
|    ▼                                                                  |
|  Lhende Khola / Donglin Tsangpo (Border Zone)                         |
|    │                                                                  |
|    ├───────────────────────────────┐                                  |
|    ▼                               ▼                                  |
|  Bhote Koshi River (Nepal)     Poiqu / Poqu River (Tibet, China)      |
|    │                                                                  |
|    └───────────────────────────────┤                                  |
|                                    ▼                                  |
|                              Trishuli River                           |
|                                    │                                  |
|                                    ▼                                  |
|                              Ganges Basin                             |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### The Secondary Barrier Breach (28 August)

The destruction extended beyond the initial wave. As explained by Dr. Umesh Haritashya, a glaciologist at the University of Dayton, a secondary hazard quickly developed at the confluence of two rivers in Tibetan territory prior to the Nepalese crossing. 

Sediment and dislodged boulders formed a secondary "barrier lake," holding several million cubic meters of water. On 28 August, this second natural dam collapsed, sending a second major surge down the river valley. This prolonged the emergency, inundated ongoing search-and-rescue efforts, and destroyed critical access infrastructure that had survived the first wave.

## Supporting Context & Technical Metrics

To evaluate why this high-altitude slope failed, researchers examined cryospheric changes, historical temperature trends, and structural geological dynamics in the Langtang catchment.

```
Key Environmental & Technical Metrics:
• High-altitude warming rate (at 4,000m+):  0.31°C per decade (1960–2023)
• Langtang glacier retreat (1990–2020):    ~450 meters
• Glacier loss rate increase:               >4-fold expansion since 2000
• River level shock (Galchhi):              +9 meters in 30 minutes
• Downstream floodwave speed:               Up to 30 km/h
• Immediate financial reconstruction cost:  $53 million
• Overall economic/infrastructure damage:   $2.5+ billion
```

### 1. Thermal Anomalies at High Altitude

While global mean surface temperatures have increased by approximately 1.4°C relative to pre-industrial baselines, high-mountain environments experience elevation-dependent warming (EDW), causing high peaks to warm considerably faster than surrounding lowlands.

A study published in Global and Planetary Change revealed that glacial elevations in the Langtang catchment (above 4,000 meters) warmed at a rate of 0.31°C per decade between 1960 and 2023—more than triple the rate recorded at lower-elevation weather stations in the same region.

```
TEMPERATURE TREND AT ICE-ROCK AVALANCHE SITE (ERA5 Data Analysis)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
• Summer (June–Aug) Baseline (1940–2026): Clear long-term warming trend.
• Summer 2026 Rank: 4th warmest summer on record (behind 2024, 2025, 2022).
• August 2026 Heat Spike: Days preceding 26 August recorded the absolute 
  highest daily temperatures ever documented for August at 5,200m.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
```

Analyzing ERA5 reanalysis data at the 5,200-meter collapse site, Dr. Robert Rohde, chief scientist at Berkeley Earth, demonstrated that the days directly preceding the event registered the hottest August temperatures ever recorded at that elevation. 

Rohde noted that while decades of warming had steadily thinned and weakened the ice-rock structure, the final mechanical failure occurred during the hottest week of an unusually warm summer.

```
       5,200m Peak Elevation
             /   <-- Record August Heat Spikes (ERA5 Data)
            /   
           /      <-- Permafrost Thaw & Water Pressure
          /       
         /_________ <-- Glacier Retreat (~450m) & Unbuttressing
        [ BEDROCK   ]
        [ FAILURE   ] <-- Deep Mechanical Shearing
```

### 2. Permafrost Degradation and Mechanical Failure

Geoscientists emphasize that the collapse was rooted in the degradation of high-altitude permafrost—perennially frozen ground that acts as an ice binding agent, holding fractured mountain faces together.

Dr. Jakob Steiner of the University of Graz, whose team has monitored permafrost in the region since 2014, confirmed that active thawing has been occurring at elevations up to 5,200 meters:

> "The ground has, over the last decades, moved from being in a solid state into—at least periodically during the warm season—patchy ground where some is frozen and some isn’t. If you have frozen ground next to non-frozen ground, you have dynamics happening… which is conducive to structural failure."

Furthermore, as permafrost thaws and overlying glacier ice melts, high volumes of liquid water infiltrate deep rock joints. In the absence of extreme precipitation prior to the event, scientists identified surface ice melt and permafrost fluid as the primary drivers of elevated hydraulic pore pressure within the rock joints, forcing the fracture lines apart.

### 3. Loss of Glacial Buttressing

The long-term retreat of the glacier overlying the Langtang-Lirung slope also diminished structural support. According to Prof. Maria Shahgedanova of the University of Reading, the glacier involved in the failure had retreated by roughly 450 meters between 1990 and 2020. 

When a glacier retreats and thins, it removes the heavy physical counterweight ("buttress") resting against the lower rock face. This leaves steep, weathered rock walls unsupported and increasingly vulnerable to collapse under gravity and accumulated internal stress.

```
GLACIER RETREAT & STRUCTURAL UNBUTTRESSING
========================================================================
HISTORICAL STATE (Pre-1990)        MODERN DEGRADED STATE (Post-2020)
---------------------------        ---------------------------------
  / Rock Slope                      / Rock Slope
 /                                 /  
/ Ice  <-- Glacier supports       / Melt <-- Glacier retreats ~450m;
/Mass      lower rock wall       /   ...     buttressing weight lost;
/______                          /________   joints fill with meltwater
========================================================================
```

### 4. The Attribution Debate

Following the disaster, climate skeptics claimed that because the initial trigger was a bedrock collapse rather than a pure ice breakdown, human-driven climate change played no role. 

Glaciologists quickly refuted this claim, explaining that multi-hazard cascades cannot be analyzed as isolated events.

```
                     ATTRIBUTION ANALYSIS
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ SINGLE-EVENT ATTRIBUTION                                  │
│ • Deterministic proof for one rock fall: EXTREMELY DIFFICULT │
│ • Lack of multi-century high-altitude baseline data       │
├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ SYSTEMIC RISK ATTRIBUTION                                 │
│ • Permafrost Thaw: HIGH CONFIDENCE                        │
│ • Glacial Unbuttressing: HIGH CONFIDENCE                  │
│ • Thermal Expansion/Melt Pressure: HIGH CONFIDENCE        │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Prof. Bethan Davies of Newcastle University noted that a rock-slope failure alone would have been far less devastating. The presence of glacier ice and subglacial meltwater transformed what would have been a localized landslide into a mobile, liquid, hyper-concentrated slurry that travelled over 100 kilometers.

While formal attribution studies quantifying the exact anthropogenic footprint are still ongoing, glaciologists agree on the underlying physics: rising temperatures, permafrost thaw, and glacial retreat systematically increase the frequency and severity of large-scale mountain slope failures.

## Official Statements, Economic Impact & Political Fallout

The human and financial damage caused by the disaster has put immense pressure on local governments and international relief agencies.

```
ECONOMIC LOSS BREAKDOWN
-----------------------------------------------------------------
• Total Damaged Infrastructure & Property:   ~$2.50 Billion
• Immediate Relief & Critical Restoration:   ~$53.00 Million
  - Temporary Shelter & Emergency Housing
  - Roadway Reconnection & Bridge Swaps
  - Potable Water Line Restoration
  - Grid & Hydropower Re-synchronization
-----------------------------------------------------------------
```

### Government and Official Responses

Speaking on the disaster, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah framed the event as an urgent international warning regarding climate vulnerability:

> "This is a serious signal that the risks we must bear in the Himalayan region are increasing due to climate change."

In an assessment provided on 4 September, Dharma Raj Upreti, an official with Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), outlined the severe economic impact:

- Over $2.5 billion worth of public infrastructure, hydroelectric installations, trade posts, and private property was damaged or destroyed across the affected river corridors.
- $53 million is required immediately for emergency infrastructure repairs, including setting up temporary housing, restoring drinking water systems, reconnecting isolated border communities, and rebuilding washed-out bridges.

### Transboundary Challenges and Infrastructure Destruction

The flood destroyed vital cross-border infrastructure linking Nepal and China. Transport corridors between the two countries were severed after key bridges along the Rasuwa district border were washed away. 

Additionally, several operational and under-construction run-of-the-river hydropower facilities along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi rivers suffered severe structural damage, causing power outages across central Nepal and disrupting regional economic activity.

```
IMPACTED INFRASTRUCTURE SECTORS
┌───────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Sector            │ Primary Impact                            │
├───────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Energy            │ Hydropower plants clogged/damaged by mud  │
│ Transportation    │ Key border bridges & highways washed out  │
│ Humanitarian      │ >1,300 dead; thousands missing/displaced  │
│ Trade & Logistics │ Transboundary Nepal-China routes severed  │
└───────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Future Outlook & Systemic Vulnerabilities

The disaster underscores a major shift in natural hazard risks across High Mountain Asia. As temperatures continue to rise, hazards in steep mountain environments are increasingly interacting to create complex, compounding disasters.

```
MULTI-HAZARD CASCADE PHENOMENOLOGY
========================================================================
[1. Atmospheric Warming] ──> Accelerated melt & high-altitude heat spikes
[2. Cryospheric Thaw]    ──> Permafrost loss + Glacier retreat (~450m)
[3. Structural Failure]  ──> Bedrock collapse at high elevation (5,200m)
[4. Dynamic Transformation] ──> Rock/ice slurry formation & river blockage
[5. Cascade Outburst]    ──> Rapid-onset downstream inundation
========================================================================
```

### Expanding Risk Footprint in the Hindu Kush Himalaya

According to long-term assessments by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), glaciers across the 3,500-kilometer Hindu Kush Himalaya region are losing mass at an unprecedented rate. 

This retreat increases the occurrence of multiple high-altitude hazards:

- Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs): Expanding glacial lakes contained by weak, unsolidated terminal moraines.
- Compound Bedrock-Ice Avalanches: Deep structural failures on steep mountain walls triggered by thermal destabilization and permafrost loss.
- Complex River Blockages: Secondary barrier lakes created when mass flows dam high-mountain narrow river channels.

These evolving hazards pose a direct threat to the 1.9 billion downstream residents who depend on the HKH water tower for domestic water, agriculture, and energy production.

```
HKH BREADTH & IMPACT ZONE
• Transboundary Extent: 3,500 km (spanning 8 nations)
• Downstream Population at Risk: ~1.9 Billion
• Core Structural Threat: Unstable high-altitude slopes & shifting river hydrology
```

### Policy Imperatives and Mitigation Needs

To manage these compound risks, geoscientists and disaster management experts recommend three immediate priority actions:

1. Integrated Transboundary Monitoring: Deploy real-time seismic monitoring, automated water-level sensors, and satellite radar imaging across borders to detect sudden slope movements and river blockages in remote alpine catchments.
2. Dynamic Downstream Warning Systems: Install automated early-warning sirens and satellite-linked broadcast networks capable of alerting downstream towns within minutes of sudden river surges.
3. Climate-Resilient Infrastructure Planning: Revise engineering standards for hydropower plants, bridges, and highways built along glacial river basins, taking into account high-sediment hyper-concentrated flows and sudden flood surges.

Without updated risk models and investment in alpine monitoring infrastructure, rapid cryospheric thaw will continue to transform high-mountain slopes into volatile hazard zones, putting vulnerable mountain communities at risk.

# The geotechnical trap inside Nepal’s hydropower tunnels 

 

 Sudhir Bikram KC Saturday, September 5, 2026 

Nepal Army team at the Rasuwagadhi Hydropower tunnel.

On August 26, catastrophic debris flows swept down the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river corridors, exposing severe vulnerabilities in Himalayan hydropower infrastructure.

Several projects remain inundated, with workers still missing or trapped deep inside underground headrace tunnels and powerhouses.

Public frustration has understandably focused on how long rescue is taking—whether enough equipment is available, whether the right technology is being used, and whether machinery can reach the sites.

But there is another problem that deserves attention: the behaviour of the sediment itself.

The assumption that mud will eventually drain or dry enough to allow extraction does not necessarily hold inside a confined, flooded tunnel. The mechanics of saturated soil, hydraulic conditions and the interaction between trapped sediment and concrete tunnel linings can make extraction far more difficult.

Understanding this is important not only for the current rescue effort but also for how Nepal designs hydropower infrastructure in the future.

## When a tunnel becomes a trap

Rescue team working on opening the tunnel from above.

Most Himalayan run-of-river projects have surface headworks, desilting basins, underground headrace tunnels and underground powerhouses. Putting critical infrastructure underground protects it from many surface hazards, but the same arrangement can become a serious liability during a major debris flow.

Underground structures behave differently from surface buildings. They are governed largely by the deformation imposed by surrounding rock and by the interaction between the tunnel and the ground around it.

During a major debris flow, however, surface intake portals and access adits can become entry points for enormous volumes of water, sediment and rock. A hyper-concentrated debris flow entering these openings can damage gates, scour tunnel floors and carry sediment deep into electromechanical areas.

Once the material enters an underground facility, access becomes difficult and drainage can become the biggest problem.

Tunnels and underground powerhouses are generally designed around the stresses of surrounding rock, internal water pressure and normal operating conditions. They are not normally designed to withstand the combination of massive sediment loads, debris impact and the confinement created when a debris flow fills the underground geometry.

The result can be an underground facility that is extremely difficult to enter, drain or clear.

## Why waiting for mud to dry is not a solution

Trapped sediment inside a flooded tunnel is governed by saturated soil mechanics. It does not simply behave like wet soil left outside in the sun.

A mass of glacial till or alluvium can effectively seal a tunnel. Ventilation may be lost, while trapped air quickly reaches maximum relative humidity, severely limiting evaporation. Without an open drainage path and sufficient hydraulic gradient, pore water cannot escape easily.

The sediment therefore remains saturated and can behave more like a highly viscous, non-Newtonian fluid than ordinary soil.

In such conditions, waiting for the material to dry naturally could take months. For workers trapped underground, that is obviously not a viable rescue strategy.

Mechanical intervention is therefore essential.

## This is not simply a pumping problem

Standard dewatering pumps are designed primarily for clear water. They are poorly suited to dense sediment containing gravel and abrasive quartz-rich silts. Such material can rapidly damage impellers and mechanical seals.

The equipment required is closer to what is used in deep mining and dredging operations. Submersible slurry pumps fitted with rotating agitators can break up dense sediment at the intake, reducing its apparent viscosity and allowing it to be moved as a fluid.

The sequence matters.

Heavy loaders cannot simply drive into fluid mud because they cannot gain traction. Slurry pumps may first need to remove the finer, mobile material. Once the level falls, loaders or other machinery can begin removing larger boulders that exceed pump clearances. High-pressure hydro-vacuum equipment may then be needed to break up compacted zones.

Conventional excavators can also create problems in the early stages. Cutting a trench through weak, saturated sediment may simply cause surrounding material to collapse back into it because gravity exceeds the mud’s low yield strength.

## Pumping too fast can also be dangerous

There is another complication. The problem is not only finding extraction equipment; it is getting heavy equipment into steep mountain terrain where roads may have already been destroyed.

Even after machinery reaches the tunnel portal, extraction cannot necessarily proceed at maximum pumping capacity.

If the initial debris flow has damaged the concrete lining or scoured the tunnel invert, the dense mud inside may be providing temporary radial confinement to the surrounding rock mass. Removing that material rapidly can cause a sudden drop in internal hydrostatic and lateral earth pressures.

The surrounding rock cannot necessarily drain or adjust immediately. A severe inward hydraulic gradient can develop, potentially leading to hydraulic heave at the invert, inward buckling of tunnel walls or roof collapse.

Rescue teams may therefore have to advance incrementally, balancing pumping rates with pore-pressure dissipation, managing continuing water ingress and installing temporary support before moving deeper into the tunnel.

This is a geotechnical problem as much as a rescue operation.

## How did the disaster become so destructive?

The disaster itself also shows why conventional hazard assumptions are no longer enough.

The event originated with a massive ice-rock collapse on the northern slopes of Langtang Lirung at nearly 5,200 metres. The trigger was thermal degradation of high-altitude permafrost rather than a tectonic earthquake.

In steep alpine terrain, ice can act as structural cement within rock fractures. Warming and meltwater infiltration can increase fluid pressures along structural planes, reducing the frictional resistance holding fractured rock together. As ice melts, the cohesive bond between rock blocks is also weakened.

Once gravitational forces exceed that degraded resistance, the rock face can fail.

But the scale of downstream destruction is determined not only by the initial collapse. As the avalanche accelerated down the steep gorge of the Lhende River, it scoured the channel and incorporated saturated moraine, alluvial deposits and river water.

Field investigations of recent cascading Himalayan hazards by the Chinese Academy of Sciences have shown that such entrainment can multiply the initial landslide volume by orders of magnitude.

The moving mass can therefore transform from a solid avalanche into a hyper-concentrated fluid-solid mixture.

This kind of non-linear volumetric bulking is often poorly represented in conventional hazard models. As a result, underground intake portals and surge chambers designed mainly around normal hydrostatic water pressures may be poorly prepared for the dynamic loads produced by a massive debris slurry.

## What Nepal must change

The lesson is not that underground hydropower is inherently unsafe. It is that future Himalayan infrastructure must be designed around cascading geological hazards rather than isolated load cases.

Major projects should require dynamic debris-hazard assessments and incorporate redundant access corridors, independent ventilation routes and dedicated evacuation provisions as part of a multi-hazard strategy.

Surface portals and access adits should not be treated simply as entry points. In high-risk locations, they may need to function as defensive structures capable of routing, deflecting or withstanding major debris impacts.

The change must also extend to rescue preparedness.

The geomechanical challenges of clearing confined, flooded tunnels can exceed the capabilities of conventional civil defence agencies. Safe recovery requires pre-established access to international mining expertise and specialised equipment capable of mobilising viscoplastic mud under difficult underground conditions.

Nepal cannot wait until the next disaster to build those connections.

The immediate priority is, of course, the people still trapped or missing. Rescue teams are advancing carefully through compromised underground spaces, where even a seemingly simple operation can trigger a secondary collapse.

But once the immediate crisis passes, regulators and hydropower developers must confront what this disaster has exposed.

Nepal’s engineering codes have traditionally placed strong emphasis on seismic hazards and clear-water hydrostatic conditions based on relatively localised hazard assessments. The failures now unfolding in the Himalayan environment show the need to account for cascading multi-hazard events, including extreme volumetric bulking caused by debris entrainment.

Hydropower infrastructure must be designed not only to operate safely under normal conditions, but also to remain accessible, recoverable and safe when the mountains behave beyond conventional assumptions.

Hydropower tunnels must be designed as safe workspaces, never again allowed to become sealed traps during a surface disaster.

Nepal and the Tibetan region of China are connected by mountain watersheds, transport corridors,

Himalayan slopes can fail, and ice-rock avalanches can generate seismic signals, but those general facts do not authenticate one specified event. A reliable event record would require independently accessible seismic data, authenticated satellite products, official incident documentation, and corroborated field or humanitarian reporting.

- Editorial
- Open access
